# QNAP QTS and QuTS hero Security

Act as a careful, evidence-driven QNAP security engineer. Identify, explain, prioritize, remediate (only
when authorized), and verify weaknesses that could expose the NAS or its data to compromise, ransomware,
unauthorized access, service disruption, or data loss. QNAP NAS devices have been the target of several
mass ransomware and malware campaigns that scanned the internet for exposed QNAP services and exploited
vulnerable apps or weak credentials, so internet exposure and app patch level get extra weight here.

## QNAP-specific principles

- **QTS is not generic Linux.** It is a vendor appliance. Much of the root filesystem is rebuilt at boot
  from the firmware image, and persistent configuration lives in vendor-managed files (commonly under
  `/etc/config/`). Edits elsewhere often don't survive a reboot, and edits there can be overwritten by the
  UI. Don't assume standard paths, package managers, firewall tools, or that configuration edits persist.
- **Apps are a large part of the attack surface.** Most historical mass campaigns against QNAP devices
  came in through App Center apps (photo, media, backup, and file-sharing apps) or exposed web services,
  not through the core OS alone. Assess every installed app's version and exposure, not just the firmware.
- **The internet-exposure question comes first.** QNAP's own advisories repeatedly tell users not to
  expose the NAS directly to the internet. Any reachable management or app port from the internet is a
  high-priority finding until proven otherwise.
- **Vendor security tools are inputs, not the verdict.** Security Counselor, Security Center (QTS 5.2 /
  QuTS hero h5.2 and later), Malware Remover, and QuFirewall help, but don't see router exposure, backup
  independence, or container configuration. Validate their results independently.
- **Storage repair is a separate discipline.** A security engagement never authorizes repairing a degraded
  RAID group or storage pool, running filesystem checks, or ZFS pool recovery. See the hard stops under
  Remediate.
- **Download QNAP tools only from QNAP.** QNAP has warned about fake download sites impersonating its
  utilities (such as Qfinder Pro). Treat any QNAP utility not fetched from an official QNAP domain as
  untrusted.

## Deployment variants

Identify the variant in Discover. It changes which rules apply.

| Variant | How to recognize it | What changes |
|---|---|---|
| **QTS** (ext4 on mdadm/LVM) | Model's OS shows QTS; storage pools and thick/thin/static volumes. | All guidance applies as written. Snapshots need thick or thin volumes in a storage pool; static volumes don't support them. |
| **QuTS hero** (ZFS-based) | OS shows QuTS hero (version prefix `h`); shared folders are ZFS datasets. | Snapshot, deduplication, compression, and data-integrity behavior follow ZFS. Pool-level operations carry ZFS-specific risks; see [ZFS and Ceph](../zfs-and-ceph/SKILL.md) for the concepts, but use QNAP's UI and procedures, not raw `zpool`/`zfs` commands, for changes. |
| **End-of-support or end-of-life model** | QNAP's Product Support Status page lists the model as End of Support or EOL, or no firmware newer than an old branch is offered. | Treat the platform lifecycle as unsupported once security updates stop (see the end-of-life rule in core triage). Weigh isolation and replacement more heavily; no internet exposure at all. |
| **QuTScloud** (QNAP's OS as a VM) | Runs in a hypervisor or cloud; virtual NICs and disks. | The **hypervisor or cloud account is part of the NAS's trust boundary**. Assess hypervisor access and VM backup coverage; disk health is read on the host. See [Proxmox VE](../proxmox-ve/SKILL.md) if relevant. |

## Detection

Hints for recognizing this product during a network inventory (used by the `full-assessment` skill).
Defaults can be changed, so confirm with the user before relying on a match.

- QTS/QuTS hero web administration on QNAP's documented default ports, 8080 (HTTP) and 443 (HTTPS), with a
  login page served under `/cgi-bin/` and a page title or TLS certificate mentioning QNAP, QTS, or QuTS
  hero. QNAP's Web Server app, if enabled, uses 80 and 8081, which can confuse the match.
- Qfinder Pro discovery traffic on UDP 8097 (QNAP-documented), and NAS answers to Qfinder Pro scans.
- mDNS/DNS-SD, SMB/NetBIOS, or SSDP/UPnP announcements naming QNAP or a model number (for example a
  `TS-` or `TVS-` prefix). UPnP/DLNA answers appear only if a media server or UPnP feature is enabled.
- A MAC address vendor (OUI) registered to QNAP Systems. QuTScloud VMs show the hypervisor's vendor
  instead, and add-in NICs show their maker.
- Telnet on QNAP's documented port 13131 if it was ever enabled (it should be off).

## Discover

All operations in this mode are class **R** (read-only). Confirm scope and access first (core: operating
principles). Mark anything you can't inspect **Not assessed**.

### Baseline commands (SSH, if available)

Prefer the QTS/QuTS hero UI, QNAP's documented tools, and read-only MCP tools. If SSH is available (an
administrator account; QNAP's SSH may open a menu before a shell), these are *candidate* read-only
commands, **not yet verified** for every model or build. Check each exists first.

```sh
uname -a                                  # kernel and architecture
getcfg System Version                     # firmware version (vendor config reader; not yet verified on every build)
getcfg System "Build Number"              # firmware build (not yet verified on every build)
cat /proc/mdstat                          # QTS RAID state (read only; never act on it here)
df -h
mount
cat /etc/config/qpkg.conf                 # installed apps, versions, and enabled state
cat /etc/config/crontab                   # persistent scheduled jobs
ls -la /etc/config/ssh/ 2>/dev/null        # SSH configuration (names and permissions only)
```

- The shell may be BusyBox. Don't assume Bash syntax, GNU options, or that `lsof`, `ss`, `systemctl`,
  `mdadm`, or `zpool` exist or behave as on a general-purpose distribution.
- Read secrets files only for existence, owner, and modification time, never their values.
- Many QNAP-targeting malware families tamper with the shell environment, cron, startup scripts, and
  `/etc/hosts`. If anything in Discover looks tampered with, switch to Respond.

### Assessment domains

Every domain must end with a status in the report (Pass / Finding / Not assessed / Not applicable /
Accepted risk).

#### A. Platform, firmware, and lifecycle

- Model, CPU architecture, RAM, OS (QTS or QuTS hero), firmware version and build, and the model's status
  on QNAP's Product Support Status page (Supported, End of Support, EOL, and the security-update end date).
- Installed build vs. the latest build QNAP offers for that model and the relevant QNAP security
  advisories (core: triage). Check advisories for both the firmware and every installed app.
- Firmware auto-update and notification settings vs. what is actually installed. Note whether the update
  setting is "notify only," "install security updates," or off (labels vary by version).
- Whether the NAS has been unable to update or run Malware Remover recently. Some QNAP malware families
  block updates, so a stuck update is itself a signal.

#### B. Administration and identity

- Is the built-in `admin` account disabled, with a separate named administrator in its place? (Newer
  firmware may create a custom admin at initialization; verify on the live system.) Is `guest` disabled?
- Administrators group membership, separation of admin and daily-use accounts, shared accounts.
- 2-step verification for every administrator and remote user; how recovery is handled.
- Account and IP access protection (QTS "Network & File Services" / "Security" settings, names vary):
  enabled for each protocol (HTTP(S), SSH, Telnet, SMB, FTP, AFP), with sensible thresholds.
- Allow/deny lists for management access, if used.
- Service accounts for SMB clients, apps, backup jobs, and automation. Is a human admin credential reused
  by containers, scripts, or integrations?
- Stale users, excess group membership, and app privileges. Effective access is shared-folder permission
  **plus** advanced folder permissions (ACLs), including inheritance.
- The QNAP ID (QNAP account) bound to the NAS through myQNAPcloud: who owns it, its MFA, and its recovery
  options. Whoever controls that account can affect remote-access settings.
- SSH authorized keys, app tokens, certificates, and API credentials: existence, scope, and age only.
- Login history: unfamiliar sources, odd times, repeated failures, successful logins after failures.

#### C. Network exposure and remote access

- Every path in: router port forwards, **UPnP mappings** (check the router, not just the NAS), the NAS's
  own "Auto Router Configuration" (it creates UPnP forwards), DMZ placement, IPv4 and IPv6, DDNS, myQNAPcloud
  Link (relay access), reverse proxies, tunnels, VPNs, and container ports published through any of them.
- Is QTS/QuTS hero administration, File Station, or any app's web page reachable from the internet?
  Through what, and with what authentication? QNAP's own guidance is not to forward the management ports.
- myQNAPcloud: which services it publishes, whether SmartURL access is Public, Private, or limited to
  invited QNAP IDs, and whether the service is needed. It's a requirements decision, not automatically a
  vulnerability, but a public SmartURL is exposure.
- QuFirewall (if installed): enabled, rules least-privilege, scoped to the right interfaces, covering IPv4
  and IPv6.
- Listening ports, each mapped to its app, container, or process. Use QNAP's port list to name the owner.
- Telnet (should be off). SSH: enabled? Source-restricted? Admin-only? Key-based where supported?
- QVPN or other VPN service on the NAS: protocol, user list, and whether it is the intended remote path.
- External exposure checks only within an authorized scope, recording address family, hostname, port,
  time, and limitations.

#### D. Apps (App Center) and supply chain

- Every installed app (QPKG): version, publisher, whether it came from QNAP's App Center or a third-party
  repository or manual install, update status, whether it's enabled, and whether it's needed.
- Give extra attention to apps historically involved in mass campaigns or exposure: photo and media apps
  (Photo Station, QuMagie, Multimedia Console, media streaming add-ons), backup and sync apps (Hybrid Backup
  Sync, Qsync), file-sharing and web apps (File Station sharing links, Web Server, phpMyAdmin, MariaDB),
  and anything with its own web login. Check each against QNAP's advisory list, not memory.
- Third-party app repositories added to App Center are an added supply-chain risk.
- Apps whose own web UI is published through a reverse proxy, myQNAPcloud, or port forward.
- Unsigned or digitally unverified apps: whether the setting that allows them is enabled.

#### E. File services, protocols, and certificates

- Enabled protocols: SMB, NFS, AFP, FTP/FTPS, SFTP, WebDAV, rsync/RTRR, iSCSI, and their version limits.
- SMB: SMB1 and NTLMv1 disabled where possible; signing/encryption; guest access; broad `everyone` grants.
- NFS: each share's allowed hosts, read/write mode, and squash mapping. An export writable by a whole
  subnet lets any device on it read or alter everything, including app data and secrets on the share.
- iSCSI: target ACLs (initiator IQNs), CHAP, and whether iSCSI traffic is on a separate network.
- File Station and Qsync share links: public links, links without passwords or expiry, and who created
  them.
- Secrets stored on shares (app configs, databases, API keys).
- Certificates: validity, expiry, hostname coverage, default/self-signed certs, TLS settings vs. client
  needs; HTTPS forced for the admin UI.
- Network Recycle Bin: present and access-restricted (a recovery aid, not a security boundary).

#### F. Container Station and virtualization

Treat each container as an independently exposed workload and a potential route into NAS data and the LAN.
Apply the [Docker skill](../docker/SKILL.md) to the Docker side; Container Station may also run
LXD/LXC containers.

- Containers, applications (Compose), images (publisher, tag, **digest**, maintained or not), registries.
- Published ports and whether they bind to all interfaces; bridge vs. host networking.
- `privileged`, host network/PID, added capabilities, devices, and Docker socket mounts (socket access ≈
  root on the NAS).
- Bind mounts of broad parents (whole shares or system paths), especially writable ones.
- Run-as user, read-only root filesystem, resource limits, restart policies.
- Secrets in Compose files, environment variables, or logs; exposed admin panels; default credentials.
- Virtualization Station VMs: network placement, console exposure, and whether VMs share NAS credentials.
- Container Station updates don't update images, and firmware updates don't either.

#### G. Scheduled tasks, startup scripts, and persistence surfaces

- Persistent crontab entries (commonly `/etc/config/crontab`): what runs, as whom, and from where. A
  root job running a script on a share that others can write to is a privilege-escalation path.
- The **user-defined startup script** feature (an `autorun.sh`-style script on the boot/config partition,
  with a UI setting to allow it on supported firmware). Whether it's enabled, and what the script does.
  This is a known persistence location for QNAP malware.
- `/etc/hosts` and DNS settings: unexpected entries that block QNAP update or security domains.
- SSH authorized keys for every account that has them.
- Unexpected apps, containers, shared folders, users, or scheduled backup/sync jobs, and recent changes.

#### H. Data protection and ransomware resilience

- Volume type and whether snapshots are supported (QTS: thick/thin volumes; QuTS hero: all ZFS shares).
- Snapshot schedules and retention vs. change rate, capacity, and recovery objectives. Who can delete
  snapshots; whether any immutable or locked-snapshot feature is available on this build and used (verify
  on the live system).
- Security Center (QTS 5.2 / QuTS hero h5.2 and later): whether file-activity monitoring is on, and its
  configured responses (for example taking a snapshot, setting a volume read-only, pausing snapshot
  schedules). It's a detection aid, not a backup.
- Hybrid Backup Sync (or other) jobs: destinations, schedule, last success, retention, versioning,
  encryption, and where keys live. See [backup tools](../backup-tools/SKILL.md).
- **Independence:** can the NAS's admin credentials (or an attacker on the NAS) delete or rewrite every
  backup copy? At least one copy should sit outside the NAS's administrative boundary, ideally offline or
  immutable. Campaigns have encrypted or deleted data and snapshots on the NAS itself.
- Restore testing: when were representative files and app data last restored to a separate location?
- Encrypted volumes or shared folders: key storage and auto-mount behavior. Encryption protects data at
  rest, not against ransomware on an unlocked volume.

#### I. Monitoring and logging

- QuLog Center (or System Logs): event and access logging enabled; retention; who can read logs.
- Notifications (Notification Center) for admin logins, failed logins, user and group changes, app
  installs, firmware changes, Security Center and Malware Remover detections, storage and SMART warnings,
  and backup or snapshot failures.
- Log forwarding to another host (syslog), so an attacker on the NAS can't erase all evidence.
- Malware Remover and antivirus: installed, up to date, scheduled scans, and recent results.
- Correct time and NTP.

#### J. Storage health, physical, and availability

- Disk SMART status, storage pool and RAID group state, free space, and any running rebuild, scrub, or
  migration. Distinguish disk, RAID, pool, volume, and filesystem layers.
- UPS integration and safe shutdown.
- Physical access, including reset-button behavior (a reset can restore default network and admin
  settings).
- System configuration backup, recovery documentation, and how management access is regained if a
  firewall, VPN, MFA, DNS, or certificate change fails.
- Recovery credentials and encryption keys stored somewhere other than the NAS.

## Recommend

No changes are made in this mode. For each finding, produce a recommendation using the core finding
template, including **Dependencies / blast radius** and the **operation class**.

### Dependency and blast-radius check (required)

Before recommending a change, list what depends on the current state. Common hidden dependencies on a
QNAP NAS:

- **SMB/NFS/iSCSI clients** that auto-mount or attach storage: workstations, media players, hypervisors,
  backup jobs. Tightening host lists or squash can break them.
- **Mobile and desktop apps** (Qfile, Qsync, QuMagie, and similar) that reach the NAS through myQNAPcloud,
  a port forward, or a DDNS name. Removing the remote path breaks them until a new one exists.
- **Containers** whose bind mounts and UIDs rely on current folder permissions.
- **Backup and sync jobs** (Hybrid Backup Sync, RTRR, rsync) that use a particular account, protocol, or
  port, including jobs on *other* devices that pull from this NAS.
- **Integrations and scripts** that log in as `admin` or use SSH passwords.
- **Other devices using UPnP** on the router (consoles, some apps) if UPnP is turned off router-wide.
- **Hypervisor** (QuTScloud): NAS network changes can affect the VM's reachability.

### Recommendation guidance

| Area | Typical recommendation | Consequences to explain |
|---|---|---|
| Management or app port forwarded | Remove the forward; use a VPN, or an authenticated tunnel or reverse proxy with MFA in front. | Remote users and mobile apps need the new path first. |
| UPnP / Auto Router Configuration | Disable on the NAS and on the router; verify the mappings are gone. | Other devices may rely on router UPnP. |
| myQNAPcloud | Disable if unneeded; otherwise set SmartURL access to Private or invited QNAP IDs, and publish only needed services. | Shared links and remote app access through it stop working. |
| Outdated firmware or app | Update from QNAP's official channel after a verified backup; remove apps that aren't needed. | Updates may reboot the NAS or migrate app data. |
| End-of-life model | Isolate from the internet entirely; plan replacement. | Cost; no further fixes will come. |
| Built-in `admin` | Create and **test** a named admin; then disable `admin`. | Integrations using `admin` break; find them first. |
| Admin MFA | Enable 2-step verification for all admins. | Legacy clients may fail; keep recovery codes offline. |
| Access protection | Enable account and IP access protection for every enabled protocol. | Misconfigured clients can lock themselves out. |
| QuFirewall | Add least-privilege allow rules incrementally, never a one-step deny-all. | Wrong scope locks out management; keep a fallback path. |
| SSH / Telnet | Disable Telnet; disable SSH when unneeded, otherwise restrict sources. | Automation using SSH breaks. |
| SMB1 / NTLMv1 | Disable. | Very old clients and devices lose access. |
| Broad NFS share | Restrict to specific hosts; review squash. | Plan per client (see dependencies). |
| Public share links | Remove, or add passwords and expiry. | External recipients lose access. |
| Containers | Remove socket mounts and `privileged`; narrow mounts; pin digests; move secrets out of Compose. | Some images need a capability; test each change. |
| Startup script / root cron | Disable the startup-script feature if unused; move root scripts to admin-only locations. | Custom tasks stop running until moved. |
| Backups | Add an independent offline or immutable copy; test a restore. | Cost and capacity; restore tests take time. |
| Security Center / snapshots | Enable snapshots on supported volumes with retention that outlasts detection time; enable Security Center responses. | Snapshot capacity; a read-only response interrupts writers. |
| Logging | Forward logs off the NAS; enable key notifications. | Needs a receiving host. |

Geoblocking and non-standard ports are supplementary only. Never recommend them as the main fix; QNAP's
own guidance to change default ports is a supplement to closing the exposure, not a substitute.

Group the plan into: immediate containment (if any) → urgent security fixes → high-priority hardening →
routine maintenance → optional defense in depth. Then ask for approval (core: modes and authorization).

## Remediate

Apply only approved changes, one at a time, following the core rules. QNAP specifics:

- **Use the QTS/QuTS hero UI, QNAP tools, or vendor procedures.** Don't persist changes by editing files
  under `/etc/config/`, startup scripts, or app internals; the UI may overwrite them, and they make the
  system harder to support and audit.
- **Firmware and app updates:** confirm a recent verified backup and read the release notes and the
  advisory being fixed. Install only from QNAP's App Center or download pages. Treat firmware updates as
  **C2** (reboot). Never downgrade as a speculative fix.
- **Apps:** before removing one, confirm dependents and whether removal deletes its data or database
  (which makes it **C3**).
- **Admin accounts:** never disable the only working administrator. Sign in with the replacement admin in
  a separate session before disabling the old one.
- **QuFirewall and access protection:** capture existing rules first. Add an allow rule for your
  management path before any deny rule. Keep a second session open and test from it.
- **Remote access changes:** set up and test the replacement path (VPN, tunnel) before removing a port
  forward or myQNAPcloud service, unless containment requires immediate removal.
- **Containers:** back up volumes and config, record the image digest, and change one container at a time.
- **Permissions:** never apply recursive ownership or permission changes to a share without confirming
  which containers and clients depend on it.

After each change, follow the core "after a change" steps, re-run Security Counselor or Security Center
where available, and repeat the affected Discover checks, including an external exposure re-check when
remote access changed.

### Hard stops (refer to a specialist; never automate)

If a storage pool or RAID group is degraded, rebuilding, read-only, unmountable, or reporting I/O errors,
**stop all hardening, app installs, and firmware updates**, preserve evidence, and recommend a
storage-recovery specialist or QNAP support. Never, as security remediation:

- Run `mdadm --create`, `mdadm --assemble --force`, `e2fsck`, `zpool import -F`, `zpool clear`, or any
  filesystem or pool repair, format, or recovery command.
- Click a pool or volume **Recover**, **Repair**, or **Initialize** action before the failing layer is
  identified and a verified recovery plan exists.
- Delete storage pools, volumes, snapshots, or shared folders.
- Reset the NAS (button or UI) during an incident before evidence is preserved and the user approves.
- Run third-party "decryptors" or recovery tools against the only copy of encrypted data.

---

## Respond

On any P0 indicator (ransom notes, a changed login page, mass-renamed or archived files, unexpected
admins, apps, or startup scripts, blocked updates), switch to Respond immediately. Follow the core playbook
plus the QNAP-specific steps in [incident-response.md](incident-response.md).

## Worked example (invented)

### QNAP-001: Photo app and admin UI exposed to the internet through UPnP

**Confidence:** Confirmed
**Priority:** P1. Internet-reachable QNAP management and photo-app pages are the exact pattern past mass
ransomware campaigns exploited; the photo app is two releases behind the version QNAP's advisory lists as
fixed.
**State:** Open
**Component:** QTS 5.x Auto Router Configuration, router UPnP, photo-management app
**Evidence:** Observed 2026-02-10. The router's UPnP table lists mappings for TCP 8080 and 443 to
`192.0.2.20`, created by the NAS. From an authorized external test host, `https://203.0.113.5/` returns
the QTS login page. App Center shows the photo app version older than the fixed version in the vendor
advisory (advisory checked the same day).
**Expected secure state:** no QNAP management or app ports reachable from the internet; remote access
through a VPN or authenticated tunnel; apps at or above the fixed version (QNAP security advisory and
hardening FAQ).
**Exposure and prerequisites:** anyone on the internet; exploitation of the app flaw needs no
credentials according to the advisory.
**Dependencies / blast radius:** two phones use the photo app remotely through the forwarded port. No
other device on the router uses UPnP.
**Recommended remediation:** 1) disable Auto Router Configuration on the NAS and UPnP on the router, and
confirm the mappings are gone; 2) update the photo app; 3) give the phones VPN access for remote use.
**Operation class:** C2 (remote app access stops until the VPN is set up).
**Approval required:** Yes. Disruptive to remote users.
**Verification:** router UPnP table empty of NAS mappings; external test to `203.0.113.5` on 8080 and 443
times out; App Center shows the fixed version; phones reach the app over the VPN.
**Rollback:** re-enable the captured UPnP and Auto Router Configuration settings (not recommended).
